title: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Russian Su-35s and Signs Up for S-400s as 50,000 Flee Its Southern Borderlands
subhead: Abiy Ahmed announced the accelerated delivery at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on the same day UNHCR said refugee flows into Kenya had jumped from 36,000 to 50,000 in 24 hours. Israel also voted to a deadlock, and the Gulf opened a direct channel to Tehran that has not yet produced a deal.

sections.heading: Ethiopia's Russian Arms Package Lands in the Middle of a Spreading War
sections.body:
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, a year earlier than the existing contract required, and will acquire four S-400 air defence batteries. He made the announcement during a two-day visit to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit, thanking Vladimir Putin for accelerating delivery. Al Jazeera and Reuters, reporting from the summit, quote Abiy saying the equipment would strengthen Ethiopia's ability to 'preemptively deter aggression'.

The timing matters more than the hardware. On the same day, UNHCR's representative for Kenya, Fatima Mohammed-Cole, said up to 50,000 people had crossed from southern Ethiopia into Kenya since clashes erupted on 20 October — up sharply from the 36,000 recorded by the agency just a day earlier. France 24 reports the fighting began after a Somali regional flag was raised in Moyale, a city administered jointly by the Somali and Oromia regions. Ethiopian forces are simultaneously engaged against rebels in Tigray and Amhara, and have pushed toward the Eritrean border in recent weeks. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov used the same summit to say Moscow is 'interested in Ethiopia and Eritrea normalising their relations'.

The Su-35 is a long-range air superiority platform; the S-400 is a strategic air defence system capable of closing airspace over a large radius. Neither is a counter-insurgency tool. Their arrival tells you what Addis Ababa is preparing for — a state-on-state contingency, most plausibly with Eritrea — rather than the internal conflicts currently generating refugees.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia has just accelerated delivery of front-line combat aircraft and strategic air defence to a government fighting three internal wars and drifting toward conflict with its neighbour. That is a durable Russian foothold on the Red Sea's western flank, at the chokepoint the Gulf war has already made more valuable.

sections.heading: Israel Votes to a Deadlock, and the Arab Parties Hold the Balance
sections.body:
With 85 percent of ballots counted, BBC News reports Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies on track for 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, against 48 for former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc. Neither is close to the 61 needed. Arab-led parties are projected at an unprecedented 19 seats and could be kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to sit with them.

Turnout was 77.7 percent, the highest in more than two decades, according to President Isaac Herzog, who said he expects official results next week before opening coalition consultations. Between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots — mostly soldiers and diplomats — are uncounted, and the early count was skewed toward areas with strong right-wing support, which analysts told the BBC means the picture can still shift. Both men claimed the mandate: Netanyahu called for 'a strong, national, right-wing government'; Eisenkot said 'the public has chosen change'.

This is not a verdict on the war. It is an election that produced no majority in a parliament where the largest opposition bloc cannot assemble one without parties most Jewish factions refuse to partner with. The scenarios now run from a narrow Netanyahu coalition to a repeat election.
sections.whyItMatters: Israel is fighting an eight-month war with Iran and a continuing campaign in the north while its government's composition is unresolved for weeks. Whoever assembles a coalition will define whether Jerusalem escalates or settles — and a caretaker government has less room to make either choice.

sections.heading: The Gulf Sends Its Defence Ministers to Tehran — and Gets a No
sections.body:
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud travelled to Tehran on Monday with officials from Pakistan and Turkiye — the three signatories of August's Mecca Joint Defence Agreement — plus Qatari mediators, for the first high-level contact between Iran and the pact states since the US-Israel war began on 28 February. Al Jazeera reports the visit came days after Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities.

The diplomacy has not closed. Reuters reported that Qatari mediators presented Iran with a draft deal on Sunday; on Wednesday it quoted Iranian officials calling the Qatari ideas unacceptable and saying Tehran would show no flexibility on the nuclear file. Iran's stated terms, per Al Jazeera, are sanctions relief, an end to the US naval blockade of its ports, and guarantees against renewed attack, in exchange for resuming traffic through Hormuz. Washington wants nuclear concessions first.

Separately, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi used a lecture at Cambridge to call for a Gulf-Iran non-aggression pact in which the United States would no longer be the primary security provider. Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi of Chatham House told Al Jazeera that a regional framework is hard to see emerging 'in the coming months or even years'. China, meanwhile, announced on Tuesday it is sending an envoy to the region.
sections.whyItMatters: The Gulf states are building a security channel that bypasses Washington, at the moment Washington is threatening another round of strikes. Even if it fails, the attempt itself signals that Riyadh and Doha no longer assume American protection is the default.

sections.heading: A Kherson Ceasefire Holds, and Europe Is Told It Is Not Invited to the Next Round
sections.body:
The truce that began on Tuesday to move food and medicine into Russian-occupied Oleshky has been extended across the wider Kherson region, the BBC reports, with no breaches recorded so far. Both sides say it is being observed: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said things were proceeding 'according to plan' and credited US mediation, specifically representatives of Melania Trump, who brokered the deal alongside Pope Leo XIV. Ukrainian officials said shelling had stopped in both Kherson city and the surrounding region. Evacuations are planned for Friday, and David Arakhamia, a senior figure in Zelensky's parliamentary party, said the truce runs until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, calling it the 'largest de-escalation since 2022'.

The humanitarian window is narrow. An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself, with a few thousand more around it, without electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was destroyed in 2023. Residents told the BBC they have been cooking garden weeds.

Diplomatically, the picture is more contested. Finland's Alexander Stubb and Norway's Jonas Gahr Støre held a 90-minute call with Putin from Helsinki — rare direct contact — and said afterwards there were 'big differences in views', while Putin restated that peace requires Russia's interests be met 'fully and unconditionally'. Both leaders stressed they were not speaking for Europe. The Kremlin then said European countries would not be included in the next round of Ukraine talks, even as the UK and Netherlands pledged additional military support to Kyiv. The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively set for early November in Abu Dhabi.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is now brokering directly with Moscow, with the Vatican and a US first lady as the visible intermediaries, while telling European capitals they are spectators. A local truce is not a peace process — but the shape of the table being set is one Europe is not at.

sections.heading: Canada and the EU Launch an 'Alliance for the Future' Without Washington
sections.body:
Mark Carney hosts European Council President Antonio Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal on 29-30 October for the 21st Canada-EU summit, where the two sides are expected to launch an 'Alliance for the Future' covering trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, AI and financial services. Al Jazeera reports the summit builds on CETA, which removed duties on up to 99 percent of goods traded between them and entered into force in 2017, and follows von der Leyen's September proposal to make Canada the EU's first 'associate member' — a status Carney welcomed.

The driver is American tariff policy, which has hit both Canadian and European exports and pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its southern neighbour. Al Jazeera notes that Canada has also been exploring membership of the Europe-led Joint Expeditionary Force.

Alongside this, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates for the first time in three years on Wednesday, and the Fed held at 3.75-4 percent on a 10-2 vote six days before US midterms, citing resilient domestic spending alongside rising inflation. Two North American central banks are now moving in opposite directions into an American election.
sections.whyItMatters: A formal associate-membership track for a G7 economy is a structural change in how the EU projects outward — built explicitly as insulation from the US. It is the clearest institutional response yet to Washington's tariff campaign.

sections.heading: Britain's Budget: Paying for Rearmament With a Cost-of-Living Patch
sections.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered the first budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister three months ago. According to Al Jazeera's readout, the headline measures are a one-off 100-pound payment to 20 million households toward energy bills, an extension of the temporary VAT cut until 1 July, and a 3.9 percent rise in both the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage from April. The energy support is explicitly a response to fuel prices driven by the Hormuz closure, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil and LNG.

Defence is where the money moves the other way. Healey funded a 15 billion pound Defence Investment Plan and plugged a 4.7 billion pound gap by reprioritising other departments, and pledged 10 billion pounds in additional economic and military aid to Ukraine. He did not set out how Britain will reach NATO's 3.5 percent of GDP target by 2035, with a 3 percent interim step in 2030, deferring that to a spending review next year. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte welcomed the commitment on X. The Office for Budget Responsibility, meanwhile, forecast zero real earnings growth next year and cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1 percent from 1.5 percent.
sections.whyItMatters: Britain is funding rearmament and Ukraine aid while its independent fiscal watchdog projects stagnating living standards. That is the political arithmetic most NATO members will face within two years — and Healey has not yet said where the defence money comes from.

bottomLine: The day's most consequential move came from Moscow, not the Middle East: Ethiopia took delivery of 12 Su-35s a year ahead of schedule with S-400s to follow, while 50,000 of its citizens crossed into Kenya in a week. Russia is arming a state fighting three internal wars on the Red Sea's western shore, and the refugee surge shows those wars are worsening. Meanwhile Israel voted to a genuine deadlock with a caretaker government likely for weeks, the Gulf's defence ministers flew to Tehran and came back without a deal, and Washington set up Ukraine talks that exclude Europe. The common thread is not one crisis but several governments deciding they can no longer rely on American guarantees — and paying for alternatives with money they do not have.
